2 Chronicles 1.audience: Readers rebuilding Jerusalem after exile would see Solomon begin his reign by worshipping at the tabernacle in Gibeon and asking God for wisdom.

culture.title: A thousand burnt offerings
culture.text: Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar Bezaleel had made—an offering on a royal scale.

culture.title: Horses from Egypt and Keve
culture.text: Solomon's traders bought horses from Egypt and from Keve (the KJV's "linen yarn" in 1 Kings 10:28), usually identified with Cilicia in southern Turkey, and sold them to Hittite and Syrian kings.

2 Chronicles 2.audience: The second temple, built after the exile, also used cedar from Lebanon brought by sea to Joppa (Ezra 3:7). Readers would see the same route used for Solomon's temple.

culture.title: Payment in food
culture.text: Solomon pays Huram's woodcutters in wheat, barley, wine, and oil. Tyre was a crowded island city with little farmland and depended on imported food.

culture.title: Floats to Joppa
culture.text: Timber was floated down the coast to Joppa, the nearest port to Jerusalem, then carried up into the hills.

culture.title: A craftsman of mixed descent
culture.text: Huram sends a master craftsman whose mother was from Dan and father from Tyre, skilled in metal, stone, wood, and dyed fabrics.

2 Chronicles 3.audience: This chapter names the temple's location: Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan (2 Chronicles 3:1). Readers would connect it with Abraham's offering in the land of Moriah (Genesis 22:2).

culture.title: The most holy house
culture.text: The most holy place was a cube of twenty cubits, overlaid with fine gold—six hundred talents.

culture.title: Cherubim of carved wood
culture.text: Two great cherubim, with a combined wingspan of twenty cubits, stood in the most holy place facing inward.

2 Chronicles 4.audience: Readers knew these furnishings had been destroyed or carried to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13–17). The chapter preserves their description.

culture.title: Ten lampstands and ten tables
culture.text: Solomon's temple had ten golden lampstands and ten tables, five on each side, instead of the single lampstand and table of the tabernacle.

culture.title: The bronze altar
culture.text: The bronze altar was twenty cubits square and ten cubits high—far larger than the tabernacle's altar.

2 Chronicles 5.audience: Readers would see the ark brought into the temple, containing only the two tablets of stone (2 Chronicles 5:10). The ark was lost when Babylon destroyed the temple.

culture.title: Trumpeters and singers as one
culture.text: 120 priests sounded trumpets with Levite singers dressed in white linen, "as one, to make one sound."

culture.title: The cloud fills the house
culture.text: As at the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), the cloud of the LORD's glory filled the temple so the priests could not stand to minister.

2 Chronicles 6.audience: Solomon prays for those carried captive to a far land who pray toward Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 6:36–39). Readers who had returned from exile were the answer to that prayer.

culture.title: A bronze platform
culture.text: Solomon stands and kneels on a bronze scaffold five cubits square in the middle of the court, so all can see him.

culture.title: Spreading out hands
culture.text: Solomon spreads out his hands toward heaven—the common posture for prayer in the ancient world.

2 Chronicles 7.audience: God's answer includes the promise "If my people... shall humble themselves, and pray" (2 Chronicles 7:14). Readers who had suffered drought, locusts, and exile would hear it as addressed to them.

culture.title: The feast of dedication
culture.text: The dedication lasts seven days, followed by the seven-day feast of tabernacles and a closing solemn assembly on the eighth day.

culture.title: A byword among nations
culture.text: God warns that if Israel turns away, the temple will become "a proverb and a byword among all nations"—a warning fulfilled in its destruction.

2 Chronicles 8.audience: Solomon builds store cities and forced-labor projects, and sets the priests and Levites in their courses as David commanded. Readers would see worship ordered as David had planned.

culture.title: Tadmor
culture.text: Tadmor in the wilderness is generally identified with Palmyra, a great oasis city on the trade route across the Syrian desert.

culture.title: Pharaoh's daughter's house
culture.text: Solomon moves his Egyptian wife out of the city of David, because the places where the ark had been were holy.

2 Chronicles 9.audience: Readers living under Persian rule would see Solomon's kingdom at the height of its wealth and fame, visited by the queen of Sheba.

culture.title: Ships of Tarshish
culture.text: Solomon's fleet returned every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. "Ships of Tarshish" were large seagoing vessels.

culture.title: An ivory throne
culture.text: Solomon's throne was ivory overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions—"there was not the like made in any kingdom."

2 Chronicles 10.audience: From this chapter on, Chronicles follows only the kings of Judah. Readers, mostly from Judah and Benjamin, would trace their own history through these kings.

culture.title: Whips and scorpions
culture.text: Rehoboam says he will chastise the people "with scorpions" rather than whips—probably a whip with barbed or weighted tips.

culture.title: Stoning the tax master
culture.text: The northern tribes stone Hadoram, who was over the forced labor—a direct rejection of the king's authority.

2 Chronicles 11.audience: Priests and Levites from the north move to Judah when Jeroboam rejects them (2 Chronicles 11:13–14). Readers would see Judah become the home of true worship.

culture.title: Fortified cities
culture.text: Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin, including Lachish, Bethlehem, and Hebron, with stores of food, oil, wine, shields, and spears.

culture.title: Satyrs
culture.text: Jeroboam appoints priests for the high places, for "the devils" (goat-idols), and for the calves he made.

2 Chronicles 12.audience: Shishak's invasion appears in his own inscription at Karnak in Egypt. Readers would see Judah become a servant of Egypt for a time (2 Chronicles 12:8).

culture.title: Allies from Africa
culture.text: Shishak's army includes Lubims (Libyans), Sukkiims, and Ethiopians (Cushites), with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen.

culture.title: Brass instead of gold
culture.text: Rehoboam replaces Solomon's golden shields with bronze ones, kept by the guard and brought out when the king went to the temple.

2 Chronicles 13.audience: Abijah of Judah addresses Jeroboam's army from Mount Zemaraim. Readers would hear his claim that God's covenant with David is "a covenant of salt" (2 Chronicles 13:5).

culture.title: A covenant of salt
culture.text: Salt, used to preserve food and in sacrifices, stood for something lasting. The same phrase describes the priests' perpetual portion (Numbers 18:19).

culture.title: An ambush
culture.text: Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah's army, surrounding it front and rear.

2 Chronicles 14.audience: Asa's reign begins with ten years of peace and the removal of foreign altars. Readers would see him defeat a huge army of Zerah the Ethiopian.

culture.title: Images of the sun
culture.text: Asa removes the high places and the "images" (incense altars) from the cities of Judah.

culture.title: Plunder of herdsmen
culture.text: Asa's army strikes the tents of cattle-keepers and carries away sheep and camels in abundance.

2 Chronicles 15.audience: The prophet Azariah calls Judah to seek the LORD. Readers would see the people swear a covenant "with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets" (2 Chronicles 15:14).

culture.title: Burning an idol by the Kidron
culture.text: Asa destroys his grandmother Maachah's idol, stamps on it, and burns it at the brook Kidron, the valley east of Jerusalem.

culture.title: Immigrants from the north
culture.text: Many from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon come to Judah, "when they saw that the LORD his God was with him."

2 Chronicles 16.audience: Asa relies on Syria rather than the LORD and is rebuked by the seer Hanani. Readers would hear Hanani's words: "the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth" (2 Chronicles 16:9).

culture.title: Physicians
culture.text: In his last illness, a disease in his feet, Asa "sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians." Egyptian and Mesopotamian physicians combined remedies with spells and magic.

culture.title: A great burning
culture.text: Asa is buried with spices and "a very great burning" made for him—a fire of spices honoring a king, not cremation (compare Jeremiah 34:5).

2 Chronicles 17.audience: Jehoshaphat sends princes, Levites, and priests to teach the book of the law in the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 17:7–9). Readers would see teaching the law as part of a good king's rule.

culture.title: Teaching from a book
culture.text: The teachers carry "the book of the law of the LORD with them" from town to town. Most people heard Scripture read rather than reading it themselves.

culture.title: Tribute from neighbors
culture.text: Philistines bring presents and silver, and Arabians bring 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats—tribute in the forms each people possessed.

2 Chronicles 18.audience: Jehoshaphat allies with Ahab of Israel by marriage. This chapter repeats 1 Kings 22.

culture.title: Kings on thrones at the gate
culture.text: The two kings sit on thrones, dressed in royal robes, at the threshing floor by the gate of Samaria while the prophets prophesy.

culture.title: Horns of iron
culture.text: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes iron horns as an acted sign that the king will push back Syria.

2 Chronicles 19.audience: Jehoshaphat appoints judges in the fortified cities and a high court in Jerusalem. Readers would see justice organized under the law.

culture.title: No respect of persons
culture.text: Judges are told there is "no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts." Bribery of judges was common in the ancient world.

culture.title: Religious and civil cases
culture.text: The chief priest presides over "matters of the LORD" and the ruler of the house of Judah over "the king's matters."

2 Chronicles 20.audience: Moab, Ammon, and others invade from the east, through Engedi. Readers would see Judah fast and pray, then win without fighting.

culture.title: A national fast
culture.text: Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast throughout Judah, and people come from every city to seek the LORD at the temple.

culture.title: Singers before the army
culture.text: Singers go out ahead of the army praising, "Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever."

culture.title: The valley of Berachah
culture.text: Berachah means ‘blessing.’ The valley is named for the people's thanksgiving there.

2 Chronicles 21.audience: Jehoram of Judah marries Ahab's daughter and follows the kings of Israel. Readers would see Edom and Libnah revolt in his reign (2 Chronicles 21:8–10).

culture.title: A letter from Elijah
culture.text: A writing from the prophet Elijah condemns Jehoram. It is the only record of Elijah addressing a king of Judah.

culture.title: No burning
culture.text: Jehoram dies of a painful disease, and "his people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers"—he was denied the usual honor.

2 Chronicles 22.audience: Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, seizes the throne of Judah and kills the royal family. Readers would see David's line survive through the infant Joash.

culture.title: A queen mother's counsel
culture.text: Ahaziah's mother Athaliah "was his counsellor to do wickedly." The queen mother had real influence at court.

culture.title: Hiding a child in the temple
culture.text: Jehoshabeath, the priest Jehoiada's wife, hides Joash in a bedchamber and then in the temple for six years.

2 Chronicles 23.audience: Readers would see the priest Jehoiada lead the overthrow of Athaliah and renew the covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people.

culture.title: Weapons from the temple
culture.text: Jehoiada arms the captains with King David's spears and shields kept in the temple.

culture.title: Standing by the pillar
culture.text: The young king stands at his pillar at the entrance, the customary place for the king during ceremonies (2 Kings 23:3).

2 Chronicles 24.audience: Jesus refers to the death of Zacharias "between the temple and the altar" (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). Readers of Chronicles would know him as the son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple court.

culture.title: The tax of Moses
culture.text: Joash calls for "the collection, according to the commandment of Moses" for the tabernacle—the half-shekel of Exodus 30:12–16—to repair the temple.

culture.title: Buried among the kings
culture.text: Jehoiada the priest is buried in the city of David among the kings—an unusual honor—while Joash is not buried in the royal tombs (2 Chronicles 24:25).

2 Chronicles 25.audience: Amaziah hires soldiers from Israel and then sends them home. Readers would see him later worship the gods of the Edomites he defeated (2 Chronicles 25:14).

culture.title: Mercenaries
culture.text: Amaziah hires 100,000 soldiers from Israel for a hundred talents of silver. Hired troops were common in ancient warfare.

culture.title: Gods of the defeated
culture.text: Victorious kings sometimes took the gods of the conquered as their own, hoping for their power.

2 Chronicles 26.audience: Uzziah (also called Azariah) reigned fifty-two years. Readers knew the year of his death as the year of Isaiah's vision (Isaiah 6:1).

culture.title: Engines of war
culture.text: Uzziah makes "engines, invented by cunning men," on the towers to shoot arrows and great stones—defensive devices on the walls.

culture.title: Love of farming
culture.text: Uzziah dug wells and kept cattle, vinedressers, and farmers, "for he loved husbandry."

culture.title: Burial in a field
culture.text: As a leper, Uzziah is buried in a field near the royal tombs. A stone plaque found in Jerusalem, written in Aramaic, says Uzziah's bones were brought there.

2 Chronicles 27.audience: Jotham reigns sixteen years, builds, and subdues the Ammonites. Readers would see a brief, faithful reign between Uzziah and Ahaz.

culture.title: The wall of Ophel
culture.text: Ophel was the high part of Jerusalem between the city of David and the temple mount. Jotham builds on its wall.

2 Chronicles 28.audience: Ahaz turns to Assyria for help, closes the temple doors, and builds altars in every corner of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 28:24). Readers knew him from Isaiah's warnings (Isaiah 7).

culture.title: Captives sent home
culture.text: Israel's soldiers return Judah's captives after the prophet Oded rebukes them, clothing, feeding, and anointing them and carrying the weak on donkeys to Jericho.

culture.title: Gods of Damascus
culture.text: Ahaz sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, reasoning that they had helped Syria's kings.

2 Chronicles 29.audience: Hezekiah reopens and cleanses the temple in his first month. Readers who had rebuilt the temple after exile would recognize the work of restoring worship.

culture.title: Cleansing in sixteen days
culture.text: Priests carry out everything unclean from the temple, and the Levites carry it to the brook Kidron. The work takes sixteen days.

culture.title: Instruments of David
culture.text: Levites play the instruments of David and the priests the trumpets as the burnt offering is made.

2 Chronicles 30.audience: Hezekiah invites the remnant of the northern tribes, after Assyria's conquest, to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. Readers would see some come and others mock (2 Chronicles 30:10–11).

culture.title: Passover in the second month
culture.text: The Passover is held in the second month because the priests were not ready in the first—an option the law allowed (Numbers 9:10–11).

culture.title: Runners with letters
culture.text: Couriers carry the king's letters "from city to city" through Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun.

2 Chronicles 31.audience: The people bring tithes and firstfruits in such abundance that they lie in heaps (2 Chronicles 31:6). Readers would see support for the priests and Levites restored.

culture.title: Heaps of tithes
culture.text: The heaps begin in the third month (wheat harvest) and are finished in the seventh (fruit and grape harvest).

culture.title: Storerooms
culture.text: Hezekiah prepares chambers in the temple to store the offerings and appoints Levites to distribute them.

2 Chronicles 32.audience: Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah. Readers knew this event from 2 Kings 18–19, Isaiah 36–37, and Assyrian records.

culture.title: Stopping the springs
culture.text: Hezekiah stops the water sources outside the city so the Assyrian army would find no water.

culture.title: The tunnel
culture.text: Hezekiah brings the water of Gihon down to the west side of the city of David. The 1,750-foot Siloam tunnel still carries it.

culture.title: Ambassadors from Babylon
culture.text: Babylonian envoys come "to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land," and Hezekiah shows them his treasures.

2 Chronicles 33.audience: Manasseh is taken captive to Babylon in chains, repents, and is restored (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). Readers who had returned from Babylon would find hope in his story.

culture.title: Hooks and fetters
culture.text: Assyrian captains take Manasseh "among the thorns" (with hooks) and bind him in fetters. Assyrian reliefs show captives led by hooks through the lip or nose.

culture.title: Consulting spirits
culture.text: Manasseh practices divination, enchantment, witchcraft, and consults mediums—all forbidden by the law (Deuteronomy 18:10–11).

2 Chronicles 34.audience: Josiah begins seeking God at sixteen and purges idolatry at twenty, before the book of the law is found (2 Chronicles 34:3). Readers would see a king turn the nation back to the LORD.

culture.title: Scattering dust on graves
culture.text: Josiah grinds the idols to powder and scatters it on the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.

culture.title: Reading the covenant aloud
culture.text: Josiah reads the whole book of the covenant to the people, great and small, at the temple.

2 Chronicles 35.audience: Josiah's Passover is described as the greatest since Samuel's day (2 Chronicles 35:18). Readers knew the lamentations for Josiah were still sung when Chronicles was written (2 Chronicles 35:25).

culture.title: Gifts of animals
culture.text: Josiah gives 30,000 lambs and kids and 3,000 bullocks for the people's Passover offerings, and his officials add more.

culture.title: Laments for Josiah
culture.text: Jeremiah laments for Josiah, and singing men and women still spoke of him in their laments, written "in the lamentations."

2 Chronicles 36.audience: The book ends with Cyrus' decree allowing the exiles to return (2 Chronicles 36:22–23), the same words that open Ezra. Readers were the people who had answered that call.

culture.title: The land's sabbaths
culture.text: The land lay desolate "until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths"—the sabbath years Israel had neglected (Leviticus 26:34–35).

culture.title: Persian royal decrees
culture.text: Cyrus allowed deported peoples to return home and rebuild their temples. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription, describes this policy.
